facts.title: Named After a Gemstone
facts.text: Beryllium was first isolated as an oxide in 1798 by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who found it while studying the minerals beryl and emerald. The name comes from beryl (via the Greek 'beryllos'), the mineral family that includes emerald and aquamarine. The pure metal wasn't produced until 1828, when Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy independently reduced beryllium chloride with potassium.

facts.title: It Once Had a Sweet Name
facts.text: For much of the 1800s the element was called 'glucinium' (symbol Gl), from the Greek 'glykys' meaning sweet, because many of its salts taste sweet. The name beryllium eventually won out and was made official by IUPAC in 1949. Despite the sweet taste, beryllium compounds are highly toxic and should never be tasted.

facts.title: Astonishingly Stiff and Light
facts.text: Beryllium is remarkably rigid: its stiffness-to-weight ratio (specific stiffness) is roughly six times greater than that of steel. It has a very high melting point of about 1287 degrees Celsius yet a low density of only 1.85 grams per cubic centimetre, lighter than aluminium. These properties make it prized for precision parts that must not flex or expand under stress.

facts.title: Almost Transparent to X-Rays
facts.text: Because beryllium atoms have only four electrons, the metal barely absorbs X-rays, letting them pass through far more easily than glass or aluminium. This makes beryllium the standard material for the thin 'windows' in X-ray tubes and detectors. The same low atomic number makes it an excellent neutron reflector and moderator in nuclear reactors.

facts.title: Born in the Big Bang and Dying Stars
facts.text: Beryllium is one of the few elements with a cosmic supply problem: stars destroy it almost as fast as they make it, because beryllium-7 and beryllium-8 are extremely unstable in stellar cores. Most natural beryllium-9, the only stable isotope, is actually forged in interstellar space when high-energy cosmic rays smash into heavier atoms like carbon and oxygen, a process called spallation. This makes it one of the rarest of the light elements in the universe.

facts.title: The Particle That Revealed the Neutron
facts.text: In 1932 James Chadwick bombarded a beryllium target with alpha particles and detected a mysterious, electrically neutral radiation, which he identified as the neutron, earning him the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. Beryllium is still used today as a neutron source when combined with an alpha-emitter such as americium or polonium. This experiment fundamentally reshaped our model of the atomic nucleus.

facts.title: A Berylliosis Warning
facts.text: Inhaling beryllium dust or fumes can trigger chronic beryllium disease (berylliosis), a serious lung condition caused by an immune reaction to the metal. Even tiny exposures can sensitise susceptible people, which is why machining beryllium requires strict ventilation and protective measures. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration tightly regulates workplace beryllium exposure limits as a result.

facts.title: Sparkless Tools for Explosive Places
facts.text: Alloyed with copper, beryllium forms beryllium-copper, a material that is strong, conducts electricity well, and crucially does not throw sparks when struck. This makes beryllium-copper tools the choice for working around flammable gases in oil rigs, refineries, and gas pipelines. The alloy is also used for springs, electrical connectors, and non-magnetic precision instruments.

facts.title: Eye on the Universe
facts.text: NASA chose beryllium for the 18 hexagonal mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope because it stays dimensionally stable at the extreme cold of deep space, around minus 230 degrees Celsius. Its lightness also meant the giant 6.5-metre mirror could be launched without excessive weight. Each segment was then coated in a microscopically thin layer of gold to reflect infrared light.

facts.title: The Element With No Stable Neighbour Below
facts.text: Beryllium occupies a unique spot on the periodic table: it is the lightest alkaline-earth metal and sits in a region where nuclear stability is fragile. Beryllium-8, which would form when two helium nuclei fuse, falls apart in about a tenth of a quadrillionth of a second, a quirk that nearly blocks the path for stars to build carbon. Only the rare 'triple-alpha' process lets stars leap past this bottleneck to make the carbon life depends on.
